title: sed and awk
lead: Use sed to replace, delete and select text line by line; use awk to split lines into fields (columns), calculate and summarize log files.
objectives: You use sed with `s/old/new/`, the `g` flag, `-n` + `p`, addresses/ranges and `d`.
You know that `sed -i` changes a file permanently and make a backup first (`-i.bak`).
You select fields with awk (`$1`, `$NF`, `-F`), write conditions and compute sums and averages with `BEGIN`/`END`.
You count values in log files with awk arrays and combine awk in pipelines with `cut`, `sort`, `uniq`.

sections.title: sed: substitution (s///)
body: `sed` (stream editor) reads text line by line, applies a command and prints the result. It **does not change the file**; only `-i` does that (third section).
The most common command is `s/search/replace/`. By default only the **first** match on each line is replaced; add `g` (global) for all of them: `s/cat/dog/g`.
The delimiter does not have to be `/`. For paths like `/usr/local` use `|`: `s|/usr/local|/opt|`. A `&` in the replacement stands for the match itself; write `\&` for a literal `&`.

commands.what: Replaces the first match on each line.
commands.why: You see the result without touching the file.

commands.what: Replaces all matches on the line.
commands.where: When a word must change everywhere.
commands.why: Without `g` the second match on a line stays.

commands.what: Uses `|` as delimiter; readable for paths containing `/`.
Applies several sed commands in order.
commands.where: When one pass needs several changes.
commands.why: The file is read only once.

sections.tip: With `-E` (extended regex) `+`, `?`, `|` and `( )` work without escapes: `sed -E 's/[0-9]+/N/g' access.log`.
sections.warn: The pattern is a **regular expression**: `.` means any character. To match a dot write `\.`, otherwise `s/1.2/X/` also replaces `102`.

sections.title: sed: selecting and deleting lines
body: By default sed prints every line. `-n` turns that off; then `p` (print) prints only the lines you want. You pick lines with an **address**: a number (`2p`), a range (`1,3p`), the last line (`$p`) or a regex (`/404/p`).

`d` (delete) drops the line from the output. `/^#/d` removes comment lines, `/^$/d` blank lines, `1d` the header line. All of this affects only the **output**; the file stays the same. To save the result, redirect: `sed '/^#/d' server.conf > clean.conf`.

commands.where: To view a specific line of a big file.

commands.what: Prints lines A through B; `$` is the last line.
commands.where: To look at one section of a file.
commands.why: You get the range with one command.

commands.what: Deletes matching lines from the output.
commands.where: When stripping comment or blank lines.
commands.why: Produces the clean version of a config file.

commands.what: Skips the first line (e.g. a CSV header).
commands.where: Before processing data that has a header.
commands.why: Later tools do not mistake the header for data.

sections.tip: `-n` and `p` always go together. Alone, `sed '2p'` prints line 2 **twice** (once automatically, once by `p`).

sections.title: sed -i: editing a file in place
body: `sed -i` writes the result not to the screen but **into the file itself**. There is no undo and no trash can: a wrong regex damages the file permanently.
Rule: run without `-i` first and check the output, then run with a backup. `sed -i.bak '...' file` keeps the original as `file.bak` and works in both GNU (Linux) and BSD (macOS) sed.

**GNU/BSD difference:** on Linux `sed -i 's/a/b/' f` is enough. On macOS `-i` requires a suffix; for no backup write `sed -i '' 's/a/b/' f`. If the same command behaves differently on two systems, this is why.

commands.what: Edits the file in place and saves the original as `.bak`.
commands.why: If something goes wrong you restore from the backup.
Leaves you a way back after `-i`.

commands.what: Shows the difference between two files.
commands.why: You see whether only the intended line changed.

sections.warn: `sed -i` cannot be undone. On production systems take a **backup** first. For several files (`sed -i ... *.conf`) test on one file without `-i` first.
sections.danger: With a wrong pattern, `sed -i 's/.*//' file` empties the whole file. Take a **snapshot** of your VM before destructive experiments.

sections.title: awk: fields and conditions
body: `awk` splits each line into **fields** at whitespace: `$1` is the first, `$2` the second, `$NF` the last field, `$0` the whole line. Change the separator with `-F`: for CSV use `-F,`.

A program has the form `pattern { action }`. Without a pattern it applies to every line; with one, only to matching lines: `$3 > 5000` or `/404/`. Without an action the line is printed. `NR` is the line number, `NF` the field count; `NR>1` skips the header.

`BEGIN { }` runs once before the first line, `END { }` once after the last. Ideal for sums and averages: `{ s += $3 } END { print s }`. Use `printf` for formatted output; you write the line ending yourself (`\n`).

commands.what: Prints the first field of each line.
commands.where: To take a column from logs or command output.
commands.why: `cut` trips over varying spaces, awk does not.
The only way to get the values into the right fields.

commands.what: Prints only lines that satisfy the condition.
commands.where: When selecting values over a threshold or error codes.

commands.what: Prints the result after the last line.
commands.why: One pass gives you the summary.

sections.tip: Always put the awk program in **single quotes**; otherwise the shell expands `$1` itself and awk gets an empty program.

sections.title: awk: counting and log analysis
body: awk arrays are **associative** (key → value) and need no declaration. `c[$2]++` increments the counter for each status code; in the `END` block `for (k in c)` prints them all. The order is undefined, so append `sort`.

The pattern combines with pipes: `ps aux | awk 'NR>1 {print $1}' | sort | uniq -c` shows how many processes each user has. `cut -d' ' -f2 access.log | sort | uniq -c` works too, but with irregular spacing awk is safer.

commands.cmd: awk '{c[$2]++} END {for (k in c) print k, c[k]}'
commands.what: Counts how often each value in field two occurs.
commands.where: When counting per HTTP status code or IP.
commands.why: Summarizes a log with one command.
commands.example: awk '{c[$2]++} END {for (k in c) print k, c[k]}' access.log | sort

commands.what: Prints the last field of each line.
commands.where: For lines with a varying number of fields.
commands.why: You do not need to know the last column's number.

commands.what: Runs once before the file is read.
commands.why: Adds a title to the report output.
`print` does not give you control of format and line ending.

sections.tip: Average: `END {print s/(NR-1)}` (with a header) or a separate counter (`n++`). Watch out for division by zero on an empty file.

t01.text: Print only line 2 of `pets.txt` with sed: `sed -n '2p' pets.txt`.
t01.hint: `-n` turns off automatic printing, `2p` prints only line 2. The simulator does not run sed ('not supported'); your command is still recorded.

t02.text: Print only the first column (the IP addresses) of `access.log` with awk.
t02.hint: `awk '{print $1}' access.log` — the program belongs in single quotes.

t03.text: Predict: which names does `cut -d, -f1 employees.csv` print (same as `awk -F, '{print $1}'`)? Think first, then run it.
t03.hint: The first column is the `name` header and four names (anna, ben, cara, dan).

t04.text: You are changing the port in `server.conf`. First back it up with `cp server.conf server.conf.bak`, then run `sed -i 's/8080/9090/' server.conf`.
t04.hint: Order matters: backup first, then `-i`. Alternatively `sed -i.bak` makes the backup itself; but here the file `server.conf.bak` must exist.

t05.text: Print `server.conf` without comment lines (those starting with `#`): `sed '/^#/d' server.conf`.
t05.hint: `^#` means # at line start, `d` removes the line. The file stays unchanged.

t06.text: Broken command: `sed 's/usr/local/bin/opt/bin/' paths.txt` fails because the `/` in the path collides with the delimiter. Fix it: replace `/usr/local` with `/opt` (use `|` as delimiter).
t06.hint: `sed 's|/usr/local|/opt|' paths.txt`. The first character after `s` is the delimiter; `|`, `#` and `,` are common.

t07.text: Predict: how often does the department `it` appear in the output of `cut -d, -f2 employees.csv | sort | uniq -c`? Then run the command.
t07.hint: `uniq -c` prefixes each distinct line with its count. The `dept` header is a line too.

t08.text: Mini project: create the folder `reports`, copy `employees.csv` into it and compute the average salary in the copy with awk (skip the header): `awk -F, 'NR>1 {s+=$3; n++} END {print s/n}' reports/employees.csv`.
t08.hint: Steps: `mkdir reports`, `cp employees.csv reports/`, then awk. `NR>1` skips the header, `n` counts the rows.

t09.text: Mini project: create the folder `backup`, copy `app.conf` to `backup/app.conf`, then change `mode=dev` to `mode=prod` in `app.conf` with `sed -i`.
t09.hint: `mkdir backup`, `cp app.conf backup/app.conf`, `sed -i 's/mode=dev/mode=prod/' app.conf`. Make the backup BEFORE `-i`.

t10.text: Predict: which animal does `sed -n '3p' pets.txt` print? Verify with the equivalent `head -n 3 pets.txt | tail -n 1`.
t10.hint: Lines: cat, dog, bird, cat, fish. `head -n 3` takes the first three, `tail -n 1` the last of them.

t11.text: Challenge: with awk select only the lines of `access.log` whose status code is 404 (condition: second field is 404).
t11.hint: `awk '$2 == 404' access.log` — the pattern alone is enough; without an action the line is printed.

t12.text: Challenge: in one sed call make two replacements in `employees.csv` (with two `-e`): `it` to `IT`, `hr` to `HR`. Just print, do not change the file.

t13.text: Debug: a wrong `sed -i` broke `db.conf` (only `host=` is left). The backup `db.conf.bak` is still there. Restore the file from the backup.
t13.hint: `cp db.conf.bak db.conf`. Check with `cat db.conf`: it should show `host=localhost` and `port=5432`.

t14.text: Ticket #3601 — 'The live server needs a clean configuration: prepare a copy without comment lines as `server.live`, and keep the original as `server.conf.orig`.' (The simulator has no sed: produce the output without comments using `grep -v`; on a real system `sed '/^#/d'` does the same.)

t15.text: Ticket #3602 — 'Write the distribution of status codes in access.log to the file `status_report.txt`.' (One count per code, e.g. `3 200`.)
t15.hint: Take the second column, sort, count: `cut -d' ' -f2 access.log | sort | uniq -c > status_report.txt`. An awk array would do the same.

t16.text: Ticket #3603 — 'Calculate the total salary of the IT department.' Write it with awk: separator `,`, rows whose second field is `it`, sum the third field, print with `END`.

vm.intro: Run these commands on your own Ubuntu/Rocky/Alma VM. Everything stays in `~/lab` and your own test files. sed and awk come preinstalled on these distributions (GNU versions).

v01.title: Create the test files
v01.text: Create the following four test files in `~/lab` with `printf` and paste the line counts.

blocks.cmd:
mkdir -p ~/lab && cd ~/lab
printf 'cat
dog
bird
cat
fish
' > pets.txt
printf 'name,dept,salary
anna,it,5200
ben,hr,4100
cara,it,6100
dan,ops,3900
' > employees.csv
printf '# server config
port=8080
# debug off
debug=false
host=localhost
' > server.conf
printf '10.0.0.1 200
10.0.0.2 404
10.0.0.1 200
10.0.0.3 500
10.0.0.2 200
' > access.log
wc -l pets.txt employees.csv server.conf access.log

differs: If a count is not 5, a `printf` line is missing or has too much; check the file with `cat` and run the command again.
If you see a literal `n` instead of a newline, check the single quotes.

v02.title: sed: replace, select, delete
v02.text: Run three sed commands. The files stay unchanged, only the output differs. Paste the output.

blocks.cmd:
cd ~/lab
sed 's/cat/hamster/' pets.txt
sed -n '2,3p' pets.txt
sed '1d' employees.csv
blocks.expected:
hamster
dog
bird
hamster
fish
dog
bird
anna,it,5200
ben,hr,4100
cara,it,6100
dan,ops,3900

differs: If `cat pets.txt` still shows `cat` that is correct: without `-i` the file does not change.
No output at all? `cd ~/lab` may have failed; repeat v01.

v03.title: sed -i with a backup
v03.text: Change the port in `server.conf` with a backup and show the difference. Paste the output.

blocks.cmd:
cd ~/lab
# GNU sed (Ubuntu/Rocky/Alma); -i.bak makes a backup
sed -i.bak 's/8080/9090/' server.conf
grep port server.conf
diff server.conf.bak server.conf

differs: On macOS/BSD `-i.bak` works too; without a suffix you need `sed -i '' ...`.
If the `diff` output is empty nothing changed; check the spelling of `8080`.

v04.title: awk: column, condition, sum
v04.text: Run three awk commands on `employees.csv`: two columns, salaries over 5000, total and average.

blocks.cmd:
cd ~/lab
awk -F, 'NR>1 {print $1, $3}' employees.csv
awk -F, 'NR>1 && $3 > 5000 {print $1}' employees.csv
awk -F, 'NR>1 {s+=$3} END {printf "total=%d avg=%.1f\n", s, s/(NR-1)}' employees.csv
blocks.expected:
anna 5200
ben 4100
cara 6100
dan 3900
anna
cara
total=19300 avg=4825.0

differs: Depending on the locale the decimal separator may be `4825,0`.
If you see `total=0`, `-F,` is missing or the shell expanded `$3`; put the program in single quotes.

v05.title: Log analysis: counting
v05.text: Count the status codes in `access.log` with an awk array, find the 404 line with sed and paste the output. Optionally count running processes per user.

blocks.cmd:
cd ~/lab
awk '{c[$2]++} END {for (k in c) print k, c[k]}' access.log | sort
sed -n '/404/p' access.log
ps aux | awk 'NR>1 {print $1}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -3

differs: The numbers and users of the last command depend on your system; what matters is the `count user` format on each line.
The order of `for (k in c)` is undefined, which is why we added `sort`.

q1.q: What does `sed 's/a/b/' file` do without the `g` flag?
options: Replaces every a in the file with b
Replaces only the first a on each line with b
q1.explain: Without `g` only the first match per line is replaced; and without `-i` the file is not changed at all.

q2.q: What is the safest way to edit a configuration file in place?
q2.explain: `-i.bak` keeps the original as `file.bak`; `-i` alone cannot be undone.

options: The first field of each line
The number of fields on the line
The last field of each line
q3.explain: `NF` is the field count, `$NF` is the value of the last field.

q4.q: What is `NR>1` for in `awk -F, 'NR>1 {s+=$3} END {print s}'`?
q4.explain: `NR` is the line number; `NR>1` runs the action on every line except the header.

summary: `sed 's/old/new/g'` substitutes; `-n` + `p` selects, `d` deletes. Without `-i` the file never changes.
`sed -i` is permanent: use `-i.bak` for a backup. On macOS you need `-i ''`.
awk splits lines into fields: `$1`, `$NF`, `-F,`; calculate with `NR`, `NF`, `BEGIN`, `END`.
With the associative array `c[$2]++` you count values in logs; sort the output with `sort`.
Always put programs in single quotes and check the result on screen first.

glossary.meaning: Stream editor that processes text line by line.
Text-processing language that splits lines into fields and supports conditions, calculations and reports.
A part of a line that awk splits off at the separator: `$1`, `$2`, … `$NF`.
A number, range or regex that selects which lines a sed command applies to.
With `sed -i` the result is written into the file itself instead of the screen.
An awk array holding key-value pairs; typical for counters.
A regular expression describing a text pattern; sed and awk use it for matching.
